tytul: Pickled herring in spiced vinegar (Wisconsin Sea Grant)
wstep: This card describes home-pickled herring fillets according to Wisconsin Sea Grant and University of Minnesota Extension, kept in the refrigerator.

ostrzezenia.tekst: According to the FDA, brining and pickling can reduce the parasite hazard in fish, but they do not eliminate it.
According to the FDA, freezing and storing fish at −20 °C (−4 °F) or below for 7 days in total kills parasites.
Keep home-pickled fish in the refrigerator and eat it within 6 weeks.

akapity: JarAtlas rule (cautious): Wisconsin Sea Grant gives one general recipe for pickled fish fillets, with no separate version for rollmops or for other spices, so this card describes only that recipe; do not change the amounts of vinegar, water or salt.
According to Wisconsin Sea Grant, any species of fish can be pickled as fillets.
Buy commercially frozen fish for pickling if you can.
Wisconsin Sea Grant gives at least 4 days for fish frozen at home, but that is shorter than the FDA requirement, and a home freezer may not get cold enough; this card follows the FDA.
According to the FDA, freezing and storing at −20 °C (−4 °F) or below for 7 days in total kills parasites in fish.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): freeze the fish this way first even though the recipe later simmers it in the pickling solution.
Use distilled (white) vinegar with a guaranteed acetic acid content of at least 5%.
Use only pure pickling or canning salt, not sea salt, iodized salt or regular table salt.
Use good-quality drinking water and avoid hard water.
Brine: for each 5 pounds of fish, 2 1/2 cups of pickling or canning salt dissolved in 1 gallon of water.

Pickling solution for 10 pounds of fish: 1/4 oz bay leaves, 2 tablespoons allspice, 2 tablespoons mustard seed, 1 tablespoon whole cloves, 1 tablespoon pepper, 1–2 tablespoons hot ground dried pepper, 1/2 lb sliced onion, 2 quarts distilled vinegar and 5 cups water.
Fillet the fish, remove the skin, wash the fillets several times in clean cold water and drain them.
Slice fillets that are an inch or more thick into pieces about 1/2 inch thick.
Put the fish in the brine in a container that is not metal, and refrigerate for 12–24 hours.
Rinse the fish in cold water, cover it with undiluted distilled vinegar and refrigerate it for another 24 hours.
Combine all the pickling solution ingredients in a large kettle and bring to a boil.
Add the fish and simmer for 10 minutes, until it is easily pierced with a fork, without overcooking it.
Take the fish out, lay it in a single layer in a shallow pan and refrigerate it.
Pack the cold fish in clean glass jars, adding fresh onion slices, lemon and bay leaves if you like.
Strain the solution, bring it to a boil, pour it over the fish and close the jars at once.
Keep home-pickled fish in the refrigerator and eat it within 6 weeks.
Pasteurizing or canning pickled fish is not recommended.
Throw away pickled fish that has been in the refrigerator for more than 6 weeks.
Do not keep pickled fish out of the refrigerator for more than 2 hours, or for more than 1 hour when the temperature is above 90 °F (about 32 °C).
